National Coordinator of the National Counter-Terrorism Centre, Maj Gen Adamu Laka, has insisted that terrorism in Nigeria, especially in the North-West, is increasingly driven by economic interests rather than ideology. According to Laka, ideological motivations are no longer the primary driver of terrorism. Laka spoke during a policy roundtable on the expansion of insurgencies in the North-West and North-Central, held in Abuja on Wednesday. Laka said, “We keep on talking of ideology. What we have today is no more ideological terrorism; it’s more of economic terrorism. What is happening in the North-West is more economic than ideological.” According to Laka, military operations alone would not resolve the security crisis, but a combination of military action and non-kinetic measures involving government agencies and other stakeholders would. “The National Counter-Terrorism Centre believes that kinetic efforts alone cannot solve the issue of insecurity. It has to be a mixture of both kinetic and non-kinetic,” he said. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. According to him, security agencies were recording successes through joint operations, including an operation in Katsina State in September. Laka expressed optimism that continued collaboration among security agencies would help restore peace, noting that attention was increasingly being directed towards the North-West and North-Central regions following improvements in the North-East. “We’re making headway. There have been successes in various sectors. You can see the peace that is currently existing. There is a higher level of peace in the North-East. We are facing the North-West now, as well as the North-Central. It’s very dear to the President and Commander-in-Chief and the National Security Adviser, and we’ll do our best to ensure that peace returns to Nigeria,” he said. Also speaking, a senior researcher at the Bonn International Centre for Conflict Studies, Dr Oyewole Oginni, said armed groups in the North-West were increasingly building relationships with existing criminal networks to sustain their operations. Oginni explained that some groups negotiated with bandits, while others collaborated in kidnapping operations, including transferring abducted victims and sharing ransom proceeds. He said understanding the financial networks behind the violence was crucial to dismantling the groups. Oginni urged authorities to investigate how ransom proceeds were distributed, who supplied weapons to armed groups and the individuals benefiting from their activities. He also identified illegal mining, particularly in gold-producing areas, as a source of funding for armed groups, noting that some residents were recruited to mine for them. The researcher said kidnapping had developed into an industry involving multiple actors, with those who collected ransom payments not necessarily being the same individuals who carried out the abductions. Earlier, the Sokoto State Deputy Governor, Idris Gobir, said the state government had spent billions of naira on security infrastructure between January and August, adding that it had provided equipment to support security operations. He described insecurity as a major challenge facing the country and said the roundtable offered stakeholders an opportunity to develop strategies to restore peace.
